The premise is too horrific and too impracticable for me to buy into. A corporation acquires a baby, imprisons him for 30 years, deliberately traumatizes him by staging his father’s death, manipulates every intimate relationship he has, prevents him from leaving through phobias and coercion, and broadcasts his entire existence for profit. I get that it's a satire. But there’s a realism problem. This isn’t merely exploitative reality television. It’s a human-rights atrocity happening in public. Where are the protesters? Lawyers? Governments? Religious groups? Journalists? People trying to break into the dome? Sylvia is essentially the only person behaving the way you’d expect millions of people to behave. The movie wants the audience to make the comparison to celebrity/Hollywood/reality TV -- but for me that was asking too much. I don't think celebs or reality tv stars are victims. Truman is. The logistics also become ridiculous if you think about them for 30 seconds. The number of people required to sustain this conspiracy, the legal structure permitting it, airspace, utilities, medical care, education, sex and reproduction, emergency situations, Truman’s legal identity, outsiders getting in, employees never exposing it, governments allowing it—the movie simply says, essentially, don’t think about that. I get that people love this movie for its message and the satire. It just wasn't for me.

A fun and interesting delve into the human psyche influential enough to the point where we use it in everyday dialogue to describe any sorts of weird coincidences. Jimmy Carrey as always is a thrilling watch, even in a more serious role than he is usually given. It takes a brilliant actor to carry a film in which only one character experiences the plot and develops throughout it. The supporting cast does their work but i can't help but find them slightly underwhelming in comparison to Carrey's starpower, even if that fact comes with the nature of the role. Unfortunately, I believe this is one of those films where the concept and premise far surpasses how it is actually presented on screen. The whole plot feels like a rush to get Truman to discover the truth, rather than spending time with this pre-established world that could present a unique dynamic between characters. The execution picks up massively once the shift happens but I think the first half of the film suffers massively through it lack of eventfulness. Culturally influencial but not the masterpiece it is often told to be. 6/10

Muy buena, introduce en la vida de un hombre atrapado desde su nacimiento en una jaula de cristal donde el aspecto más feo no radica únicamente en la megalomanía de su creador sino en la complicidad de una sociedad capaz de ignorar el abuso sistemático y la privación absoluta de la libertad de un ser vivo con el único fin de mantenerse entretenida exponiendo un egoísmo social absoluto donde lo que no les afecta de forma directa no tiene relevancia para la mayoría. Esta falta de empatía colectiva funciona en mi opinión como un espejo de cómo se normaliza el cautiverio en nuestra propia realidad. Si bien a nivel legal una de estas cosas es impensable en el mundo real por al valor que le damos a nuestra propia especie, el concepto se vuelve real si pensamos por ejemplo en el encierro que sufren los animales en los zoológicos. Al igual que el protagonista ellos tienen formas de comunicación, pensamientos y emociones, no decidieron nacer en entornos artificiales ni convertirse en el espectáculo de nadie. La historia de la película nos obliga a empatizar con Truman porque es más fácil reconocer nuestra propia humanidad en él, pero al mismo tiempo es una crítica hacia la hipocresía de cómo la sociedad cancela esa misma compasión cuando se trata de otras especies del mundo y cosas que no los afectan personalmente.

The Truman show. Dirigida por Peter Weir. (1998) La película sigue a Truman Burbank, un hombre que descubre que su vida es un programa muy popular de televisión, pero debajo de esa premisa hay una película bastante inquietante sobre la libertad, la identidad, el control y nuestra necesidad de sentir que nuestra vida nos pertenece. Seahaven es prácticamente perfecto; es una pequeña isla con calles limpias, vecinos amables y casas bonitas. Todo eso está diseñado para que Truman no tenga motivos para querer irse de Seahaven. Prácticamente está encerrado por una rutina, y la manipulación constante. Su miedo al agua, por ejemplo, fue creado deliberadamente para impedirle abandonar la isla. No necesitan poner una pared delante de él si consiguen que él mismo crea que no puede atravesarla. •Al igual que Christof no se considera un villano. Él cree que le está dando a Truman una vida segura y auténtica dentro de un mundo diseñado exclusivamente para él. Y ahí está una de las partes más interesantes: Christof confunde conocer completamente a una persona con tener derecho y control sobre ella. Decide quiénes son sus amigos, quién será su esposa, dónde vivirá, qué verá y qué temerá. Incluso controla las circunstancias de sus relaciones. Es una forma extrema de paternalismo: "Yo sé qué es mejor para ti, aunque tú no lo sepas." •Sylvia es fundamental porque ella le dice, de alguna manera, que aquello que considera normal no es normal. Ella se convierte en la primera grieta de su realidad. La segunda fue sin duda la repentina aparición de su padre, el cual, en su historia, estaba muerto. En resumen. The Truman Show no trata solamente sobre un hombre que descubre que vive dentro de un programa de televisión. Trata sobre atreverse a cuestionar la realidad que nos entregaron. Y o sea fuera del tono serio, que miedo. Él realmente pensaba que se estaba volviendo loco. ¿Cómo podrías comprobarte a ti mismo que no estás alucinando cuando todos te dicen que es la realidad? Tipo, su mejor amigo desde los 7 años seguía un guión. Ay no, literalmente podría ser un episodio de black mirror. "In case I don't see ya. Good afternoon, good evening and good night" -Truman.

Jim Carrey's bombastic positivity matched with Ed Harris' flat-cap-wearing cruelty make this war over a world ...nearly enchanting. The Truman show is a rare thing, in that it gives itself away immediately, the wool is pulled back for the viewers so we, on our couches, are in step with all the characters and viewers slobbering on their couches within this world. The meta-handshake happens the moment we cue this one up. But don't be fooled, this is a film about cruelty, torture, and deception on a scale the likes of which too many of us might fail to notice hits too close to home. It is good art in the sense that this is a film that comments on something we were headed for... and now live within. Its relevance came to us, over time. So much of so much of this film is ubiquitous at this point. We watch it and shrug and fail to see that Carrey looking at himself in the mirror, ought to be us looking in the mirror. We watch him, watching himself... but the smoke and mirrors movie magic of it all is that it is us he is talking to, not himself - he is calling out for us to break out of the world we've been presented with, to question the nature of the system we live within. It doesn't hurt that he is willing to die to find the truth, a new reality, to push back against the status quo. But my lord, when you realize that he is walking into a world which has gleefully watched him be caged and lied to for a lifetime, that that is the choice he chooses... you begin to see that the overlord's offer is a better deal than its surface might suggest. This one ends where it should, before you see Carrey see people who love him vicariously, who want to meet him, who care for him as the celebrity of their own twisted obsessions to see people controlled. But maybe love is enough to blind him to reality? But once the gig is up, once the cruelty has transformed and lost its juice, us, just like those parking cops at the end, turn the channel to see what else is on.

“In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.
